persona.who: 25, Tamil-Singaporean analyst at a bank, first in family to go to university, got promoted early, feels she doesn't belong in the room.
persona.note: got promoted ahead of people with MBAs. in every meeting I think they're going to find out I'm just the girl from the HDB whose dad drove a taxi. I over prepare for everything and still feel sick before presenting

understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call not feeling good enough, and that is where this week begins.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the replaying and the sickness, named without judgement.
week_beats.steady: You hold that a promotion is something that happened, not who you are.
week_beats.story: A woman who was promoted ahead of more qualified peers shows you what standing in your own truth looks like from the inside.

understanding.core_struggle: Promoted ahead of more qualified peers, she feels like a fraud and over-prepares, yet still feels sick before presenting.
understanding.mirror: You over-prepare for the meeting, and still feel sick before you even open your mouth.
understanding.insight: The promotion is not the problem, and the preparation is not the answer. The thing that makes you sick is the sentence you keep repeating about who you are, and who your father was.

queries.hook: The weight of a promotion you don't believe you earned, and the sickness that comes before every meeting even though you are over-prepared. I feel like an imposter.
queries.diagnose: When a result goes wrong, the mind turns against itself; self-blame grows from believing the outcome alone measures our worth, and the past becomes evidence.
queries.steady: A failure is something that happened, not who you are; no one who tries to do good is ever lost.
queries.act: Lift yourself up instead of pushing yourself down; learn what this taught you, make amends where you can, and begin again.
queries.story: A woman who was promoted ahead of more qualified peers, facing her own doubt and the judgment of others, yet finding the courage to stand in her own truth.

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse.sanskrit: चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम् । तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम् ॥
verse.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.
verse.why: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

prasang.title: Mastering the mind
prasang.summary: Arjuna says the mind is restless, stormy and stubborn. Krishna agrees, and says practice and letting go can train it.
prasang.lesson: The mind is hard to hold, but practice and letting go train it.

verse.meaning: Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent and stubborn, and as hard to control as the wind. Krishna agrees, but he also says that through practice and letting go, the mind can be trained. The verse does not promise that the wind will stop blowing. It says that you can learn to steer through it.
verse.for_you: You feel sick before you present. That is the wind. The replaying of who your father was and who you are is the storm. You do not need to stop the thoughts today. You only need to notice that they are blowing through, and that you can still stand in the room while they pass.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: The poet looks back on his own youthful arrogance.
verse.sanskrit: यदा किञ्चिज्ज्ञोऽहं गज इव मदान्धः समभवम् तदा सर्वज्ञोऽस्मीत्यभवदवलिप्तं मम मनः । यदा किञ्चित्किञ्चिद्बुधजनसकाशादवगतम् तदा मूर्खोऽस्मीति ज्वर इव मदो मे व्यपगतः ॥
verse.line: When I knew a little, I thought I knew everything. Learning from the wise, my fever of pride broke.
verse.translation: When I knew a little, I was blind with pride like an elephant in rut, and my mind swelled: 'I know everything.' When, little by little, I learned from the wise, I realised 'I am a fool', and my pride left me like a fever.
verse.why: Spend your effort where it can land; some minds will not move, and the first one to check is yours.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On fools and the half-learned
prasang.summary: Twelve verses on the futility of arguing with the closed or half-educated mind, framed as satire. The poet admits his own early arrogance (Niti 8) and ends by preferring wild mountains to the company of fools.
prasang.lesson: Spend your effort where it can land; some minds will not move, and the first one to check is yours.

verse.meaning: The poet Bhartrihari looks back at his own youth and remembers how a little knowledge made him arrogant and blind. He thought he knew everything, like an elephant in rut. But slowly, by learning from wiser people, he saw his own foolishness. His pride left him like a fever breaking. The point is simple. You cannot force every mind to change, and the first mind you could check is your own.
verse.for_you: The over-preparing will not land until you let the wise in. Let the next review be a place to check your own mind, not just to prove it.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.sanskrit: पातितोऽपि कराघातैरुत्पतत्येव कन्दुकः । प्रायेण साधुवृत्तनामस्थायिन्यो विपत्तयः ॥
verse.line: A ball knocked down bounces back up. For good people, setbacks rarely last.
verse.translation: A ball struck down by the hand flies right back up. As a rule, the misfortunes of those who live rightly do not last.
verse.why: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.
verse.misuse: Not a promise that suffering is always short, or that people who suffer long did something wrong.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On steadfastness
prasang.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks from a long view, not a single moment. They have seen the mind swell with a little knowledge and then crash against what it does not know. They tell the reader that a ball struck down by a hand flies right back up. The point is that setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path. The text does not promise that pain is always short, or that long suffering means a person did something wrong.
verse.for_you: The promotion is something that happened to you, not the whole truth of who you are. Let that sentence settle. You do not have to be the person who knows everything to be the person who is good enough.

verse.speaker: Vidula
verse.setting: Queen Vidula rouses her son, who lies defeated and despairing after losing his kingdom.
verse.sanskrit: माऽऽत्मानमवमन्यस्व मैनमल्पेन बीभरः / मनः कृत्वा सुकल्याणं मा भैस्त्वं प्रतिसंहर
verse.line: Don't think less of yourself or settle for little. Set your mind on something good, and stop fearing.
verse.translation: Do not hold yourself in contempt, and do not keep it going on too little. Set your mind on what is truly good; don't be afraid. Pull yourself together.
verse.why: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

prasang.title: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.
prasang.story_hook: A prince lay in bed after losing everything, until his mother walked in and refused to let him stay there.
prasang.lesson: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

verse.for_you: A mistake is something you did, not who you are; no one who tries to do good is ever lost.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse.sanskrit: उद्धरेदात्मनाऽऽत्मानं नात्मानमवसादयेत् । आत्मैव ह्यात्मनो बन्धुरात्मैव रिपुरात्मनः ॥
verse.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.
verse.why: You can be your own best friend or worst enemy; choose friend.
verse.misuse: Not 'you're alone, so don't ask for help'. Arjuna himself asks for help; this is about not abandoning yourself.

prasang.title: Lift yourself by yourself; marks of the realised
prasang.summary: Raise yourself by yourself; you are your own friend or enemy. The self-mastered person stays calm in heat and cold, praise and blame, and sees friend and foe alike.
prasang.lesson: You can be your own best friend or worst enemy; choose friend.

verse.meaning: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna on the battlefield, in a moment when everything is uncertain. He says that you alone are your best friend or your worst enemy. You can lift yourself up by your own strength and self-respect, or you can let yourself sink into doubt. The choice is entirely yours. The truth underneath is that you do not have to wait for someone else to give you your place.
verse.for_you: Before your next presentation, stand in front of the mirror and say one true thing about your work that you know is solid. Let that be the ground you stand on.

verse.speaker: Dharmavyadha (the righteous meat-seller)
verse.setting: In Mithila, a meat-seller famed for wisdom teaches a proud ascetic what goodness really is.
verse.sanskrit: पापं चेत्पुरुषः कृत्वा कल्याणमभिपद्यते / मुच्यते सर्वपापेभ्यो महाभ्रेणेव चन्द्रमाः
verse.line: Turn to doing good after a wrong, and you come out like the moon from behind a cloud.
verse.translation: If a person who has done wrong turns to doing good, he is freed from all his wrongs, like the moon coming out from behind a great cloud.
verse.why: Wisdom lives in ordinary people doing ordinary work honestly. Care for your parents.

prasang.title: Vyadha Gita: the butcher who taught a sage
prasang.summary: A proud ascetic, Kaushika, is sent to learn from a meat-seller in Mithila. The butcher teaches him plain goodness: don't return evil, repent and resolve, keep envy away, care for your parents, and don't spend your one life making enemies.
prasang.lesson: Wisdom lives in ordinary people doing ordinary work honestly. Care for your parents.

verse.meaning: In Mithila, the meat-seller Dharmavyadha tells the proud ascetic Kaushika that goodness is not a distant idea. It is simply this: after a wrong, turn to doing good. That single turn of the heart frees you from the weight of it, like the moon emerging clear and whole from behind a heavy cloud.
verse.for_you: The shame you feel is a cloud. It hides the work you are already doing. Today, let your preparation for the presentation be the doing good. Trust that the effort itself is enough to clear the sky.

story.title: Jambavan reminds Hanuman who he is
story.story_hook: Everyone had named a number, and the one who could actually do it was sitting quietly at the back.
story.summary: At the ocean's edge, each monkey says how far he can leap; none can cross. Old Jambavan turns to Hanuman, who has sat silent, and reminds him of his birth and power: why are you holding back? This is your time. Hanuman grows and prepares to leap.
story.lesson: Sometimes you need someone to remind you what you are capable of.

anchor.speaker: Jambavan
anchor.setting: On the southern shore no one can leap the ocean; old Jambavan turns to the silent Hanuman.
anchor.sanskrit: बलं बुद्धिश्च तेजश्च सत्त्वं च हरिपुङ्गव। विशिष्टं सर्वभूतेषु किमात्मानं न सज्जसे।७।।
anchor.line: You have the strength, the brains and the courage. Why are you holding yourself back?
anchor.translation: Your strength, intelligence, energy and courage stand out among all beings, best of monkeys. Why do you not step up?
anchor.why: Sometimes you need someone to remind you what you are capable of.

prasang.title: Jambavan reminds Hanuman who he is
prasang.summary: At the ocean's edge, each monkey says how far he can leap; none can cross. Old Jambavan turns to Hanuman, who has sat silent, and reminds him of his birth and power: why are you holding back? This is your time. Hanuman grows and prepares to leap.
prasang.story_hook: Everyone had named a number, and the one who could actually do it was sitting quietly at the back.
prasang.lesson: Sometimes you need someone to remind you what you are capable of.

story.hook_title: Everyone said how far they could leap, and Hanuman sat silent at the back
story.teaser: Everyone said how far they could leap, and Hanuman sat silent at the back
story.for_you: The promotion sits in your hands. The sickness before presenting is not about the work. It is the story you tell yourself about who you are. Let someone else name your strength for you today, and see if the fear loosens its grip.

script: You are carrying the weight of a promotion that does not feel like yours. You prepared until your body ached, yet the morning of the presentation your stomach turned. You feel ashamed that you might be found out, and anxious about what comes next.

Arjuna stands on a battlefield, his heart heavy with doubt. He has just heard Krishna explain the path of inner work, and he admits his deepest fear. He tells Krishna that his mind is restless, turbulent, and stubborn, and that holding it feels as impossible as catching the wind. Arjuna said:
चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम्, तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम्.
In plain words: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.

Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent and stubborn, and as hard to control as the wind. Krishna agrees, but he also says that through practice and letting go, the mind can be trained. The verse does not promise that the wind will stop blowing. It says that you can learn to steer through it.

Today, when the thoughts about your father and your place at work begin to blow through, do not fight them. Notice them as weather passing through the room. Your job is to remain standing. The preparation was your work. Now let your body rest.
The wind is real, but so are you.

depth.life: You stand in your office, ready to present, and your stomach tightens. The thought that you were promoted ahead of more qualified peers is already running through your head, and you are trying to hold it down while your body feels sick.
depth.points: The mind is like the wind, Krishna says to Arjuna. It is strong and stubborn, and it will not simply obey you. You cannot force it to stop, but you can learn to stand steady while it blows.
depth.practice: Take a slow breath before you speak, and let the anxious thought pass without gripping it.
depth.question: Can you feel the room beneath your feet while the wind moves?
